detailed_rationale:
Engineers India Ltd (EIL) is the PSU engineering-consultancy franchise historically built around India's refinery/petrochemical capex cycle (clients include IOCL, BPCL, HPCL, ONGC and other hydrocarbon PSUs), split between a high-margin consultancy segment and a lower-margin turnkey/EPC segment. The quant data flags a growth divergence -- 3-year revenue CAGR of only 5.7% versus 1-year growth of 27.2% -- which is exactly the kind of print that needs a base-effect check before being credited.

Having done that check, the acceleration looks real rather than an artifact: FY26 revenue grew 27.1% YoY to Rs 3,849 cr and PAT grew 36.9% to Rs 638 cr, both record highs, and critically the order book grew 28.9% YoY to a record Rs 15,109 cr (consultancy is 72% of that book) -- backlog growth of this magnitude is not consistent with a mere prior-year base effect; it reflects EIL genuinely riding the current India refinery/petrochemical/energy-transition capex upcycle. Management's own FY27 guidance -- 10-15% revenue growth, stable ~Rs 8,000 cr annual order inflow, 20-25% consultancy margins -- is a deceleration from the 27% pace but still a healthy, credible forward number, and importantly it comes from the company itself rather than being my extrapolation of the trailing print.

The balance sheet is essentially debt-free (D/E 0.005, interest cover 348x) with ROE/ROCE both around 17-18%, and a PE of ~19x is undemanding for a company posting record profits and a record, well-diversified order book (management specifically calls out Middle East headwinds being offset by Africa and domestic strength). This is a case where the quant divergence flag is worth investigating but does not indicate a real problem once the order-book evidence is checked.
recommendation_rationale: Already a quant-Hold; despite the growth-divergence flag resolving in EIL's favour (real order-book-backed acceleration, not a base-effect artifact) and a reasonable valuation, there is no basis to push past Hold -- cyclicality (oil & gas capex, Middle East exposure) and PSU-consultancy revenue lumpiness argue for keeping this at Hold rather than treating it as an obvious rescue-to-Buy case (which is not in the available vocabulary regardless).
summary: Engineers India is a debt-free PSU engineering-consultancy franchise that just posted record revenue, profit, and order book on the back of India's refinery and petrochemical capex cycle. We checked whether the sharp one-year growth acceleration (versus a much slower 3-year average) was a one-off base effect, and it was not -- the order book itself grew nearly 29% to a record high, and management's own guidance points to continued, if more moderate, growth next year. We rate this a Hold: fundamentals are genuinely improving, but the valuation already reflects a good part of that, and the business remains tied to lumpy, cyclical energy-sector capex decisions.
positive_para: Record FY26 revenue (+27%), profit (+37%), and order book (+29% YoY to Rs 15,109 cr, of which 72% is higher-margin consultancy) -- a genuine, order-book-verified acceleration rather than a base-effect illusion. Debt-free balance sheet, ROE/ROCE both around 17-18%, and explicit management guidance (10-15% revenue growth, stable order inflow, 20-25% consultancy margins) for FY27 gives unusually good forward visibility for a PSU consultancy.
negative_para: Revenue and order inflow are tied to lumpy hydrocarbon/petrochemical capex decisions by PSU oil companies and Middle East national oil companies -- management itself flags Middle East headwinds, being offset for now by Africa and domestic demand, but a reversal of that offset would slow order inflow quickly. The business's own 3-year CAGR (5.7%) is a reminder that the current 27% pace has, in the past, given way to multi-year slow patches.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~19x earnings, the market is pricing continuation of the current capex supercycle at something close to management's own 10-15% guided pace -- a reasonable, not aggressive, assumption given the record and well-diversified order book. Fair value given the order-book evidence, with upside if Africa/domestic order inflow more than offsets the acknowledged Middle East softness.
